## Learning Objectives
By the end of this practical lab you will be able to:

* Retrieve and process OpenStreetMap (OSM) data with `osmdata`
* Work with OSM features as `sf` objects
* Visualize OSM data as a multi-layer interactive map with `leaflet`
* Export a `leaflet` map as a static HTML file you can open in any browser
* Host the map on GitHub Pages so anyone can view it with a link

**CHEATSHEETS!** You are encouraged to download RStudio Cheatsheets. You can find them on RStudio website [here](https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/?type=posit-cheatsheets/), or a comprehensive list (more than what has been listed) [here](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/). For example, here you can find [base R syntax](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/base-r.pdf), [dplyr](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-transformation.pdf), [sf](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/sf.pdf), and [leaflet](https://ugoproto.github.io/ugo_r_doc/pdf/leaflet-cheat-sheet.pdf).

Functions                     | Package     | Task
-------------------------------|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------
`getbb()`                      | osmdata     | Retrieve a place boundary by place name (returns a bounding box)
`opq()`                        | osmdata     | Build an Overpass query from a bounding box
`add_osm_feature()`            | osmdata     | Add a single key-value tag to an Overpass query
`add_osm_features()`           | osmdata     | Add several key-value tags to an Overpass query in one call
`osmdata_sf()`                 | osmdata     | Run an Overpass query and return the result as `sf` objects
`st_make_valid()`              | sf          | Repair invalid geometries before mapping or spatial analysis
`leaflet()`                    | leaflet     | Initialize a Leaflet map
`addTiles()`                   | leaflet     | Add a basemap tile layer (default OSM, or a custom `urlTemplate`)
`addPolygons()` / `addPolylines()` / `addCircleMarkers()` | leaflet | Add polygon / line / point layers to a map
`addLegend()`                  | leaflet     | Add a legend for a data variable
`addLayersControl()`           | leaflet     | Add controls for turning map layers on and off
`saveWidget()`                 | htmlwidgets | Export a leaflet map as a standalone HTML file

For **Python** users, `OSMnx` and `Folium` provide the same OSM-retrieval-and-interactive-mapping workflow shown in this lab.

`osmdata` queries OpenStreetMap features directly from the Overpass API using a place name or bounding box, and returns them as `sf` objects. `leaflet` builds interactive Leaflet.js web maps from those `sf` objects and exports them as standalone HTML, which makes them easy to host on a static site like GitHub Pages.

## Setting Environment, Libraries, and Data

Install the Lab 9 packages (once):
```{r eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c('osmdata', 'leaflet', 'htmlwidgets'))
```

```{r message=FALSE}
#replace my path with yours to the Lab 9 folder
setwd("/Users/xfliang/University of Michigan Dropbox/Xiaofan Liang/UM_Teaching/URP535_Urban_Informatics/F26/Lab/Lab9/")

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(osmdata)     # queries OpenStreetMap features from the Overpass API
library(leaflet)     # builds interactive Leaflet web maps
library(htmlwidgets) # exports a leaflet map as a standalone HTML file
```

This lab queries OpenStreetMap data live for the University of Michigan North Campus area -- no local data files are needed.

## Retrieve OSM Data on UMich North Campus

OSM data has three geometry types: **Node**, **Way**, and **Relation**. A node can be a point of interest, but it can also be a vertex that forms the geometry of a polygon. A way can be a line or polygon, such as a road or building. A relation is a collection of nodes, ways, and other relations, such as a bus line or administrative boundary. In this lab, we mostly work with nodes and ways.

There are two steps for downloading OSM data:

1. Determine the **bounding box** for the download.
2. Tell OSM what **features** (key-value tags) you want -- amenities, roads, buildings -- and convert the result into `sf` objects.

### Step 1: Determine the Bounding Box

An OSM query starts with a bounding box. `getbb()` uses the free Nominatim API provided by OpenStreetMap to find the bounding box associated with a place name. It is recommended to double-check the returned bounding box, because many places share similar names.

```{r}
getbb("Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA")
getbb("University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA")
```

Note: If getbb() returns the error `'curl_modify_url' is not an exported object from 'namespace:curl'`, your installed curl package is likely outdated. The required function was introduced in curl version 6.3.0. To resolve this, update the package using `install.packages("curl")`. If R asks `"Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?"`, select Yes. This installs a newer version that your computer needs to compile, which may require additional tools (Rtools on Windows or Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS). 

After installation, restart your R session and verify that the function is available:

`"curl_modify_url" %in% getNamespaceExports("curl")`

If this returns `TRUE`, retry the `getbb` commands. If the installation process fails, seek support from the GSI.


You can also supply four coordinates directly as `c(xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax)`. You can get `xmin`/`ymin` by clicking the bottom-left corner of your area of interest in Google Maps (or another map interface), and `xmax`/`ymax` from the top-right corner. Since "North Campus" isn't a well-defined place name in OSM, we use a numeric bounding box for it instead.

```{r}
# Roughly the bottom-left and top-right corners of UM North Campus.
bbox <- c(-83.725706, 42.287305, -83.704518, 42.302508)
bbox
```

### Step 2: Add OSM Features and Convert to `sf` Objects

OSM features are stored as **key-value** (or **feature-value**) pairs. To retrieve restaurants, you'd use `key='amenity'`, `value='restaurant'`. `add_osm_feature()` adds a single key-value pair to a query; `add_osm_features()` adds several at once. Without a `value`, `osmdata` retrieves **all** values under that key.

**How do you find out what key-value pairs exist?**

- The [OSM Wiki Map Features page](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Map_features) covers most commonly used pairs, with definitions for each.
- `available_features()` and `available_tags()` in `osmdata` cover the same information as the Map Features page.
- [Taginfo](https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/) shows how many instances of a key-value pair exist -- useful for checking whether a tag is common enough, or is only used in a specific local context.
- Google your interest together with "OSM." Searching "restaurant in OSM" turns up the [amenity=restaurant](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:amenity%3Drestaurant) page directly.

We retrieve three layers this way: **buildings**, **roads**, and **amenities**.

#### Buildings

`key = 'building'` retrieves every building-tagged feature. The result comes back split across `osm_points`, `osm_lines`, and `osm_polygons` (a node may carry building-related tags even though the polygon is what we want), so we keep only `osm_polygons`. OSM polygons occasionally have minor topology errors (such as not closing correctly); `st_make_valid()` from `sf` repairs those before mapping. We also drop down to just the `geometry` column -- OSM features come back with dozens of tag columns we don't need for this map, and keeping them increases the size of the exported file.

```{r}
building <- opq(bbox = bbox) %>% 
  add_osm_feature(key = 'building') %>%
  osmdata_sf()

building

# Keep only the polygons, fix any invalid geometries, and drop down to just geometry.
building_polygons <- building$osm_polygons %>%
  st_make_valid() %>%
  select(geometry)

nrow(building_polygons)
head(building_polygons)
```

#### Roads

Roads are stored under the `highway` key. In OSM, `highway` covers all road-like features -- residential streets, service roads, footways, cycleways, paths -- not just highways in the everyday sense. `key = 'highway'` retrieves all of them; we keep `osm_lines` and, again, trim to just the columns the map actually uses.

```{r}
roads <- opq(bbox = bbox) %>%
  add_osm_feature(key = 'highway') %>%
  osmdata_sf()

roads_lines <- roads$osm_lines %>% select(highway, geometry)

nrow(roads_lines)
head(roads_lines)
```

#### Amenities

We retrieve several food-and-drink amenity types in one query with `add_osm_features()`, then keep point geometries. A few amenities are mapped as building polygons rather than points (e.g. a whole food court); `st_centroid()` converts those to points so they can join the same layer -- you may see a warning that attributes are assumed constant over each geometry, which is safe to ignore since we only keep the resulting point location. Many OSM points are missing a `name`, which would leave the map's popup blank. We drop those here to keep the demo map focused on labeled points, though in a real analysis you'd usually keep unnamed points too.

```{r}
amenity <- opq(bbox = bbox) %>%
  add_osm_features(features = c(
    "amenity" = "restaurant",
    "amenity" = "bar",
    "amenity" = "biergarten",
    "amenity" = "fast_food",
    "amenity" = "food_court",
    "amenity" = "cafe",
    "amenity" = "pub",
    "amenity" = "ice_cream"
  )) %>%
  osmdata_sf()

# Convert polygon amenities to centroids before combining with the point amenities.
amenity_points <- amenity$osm_points
amenity_polys <- bind_rows(
        amenity$osm_polygons,
        amenity$osm_multipolygons
    ) %>%
    st_centroid()

# Combine points and centroids, keep only the relevant columns, and drop entries
# missing a name (so only named places remain).
amenity_point <- bind_rows(amenity_points, amenity_polys) %>%
  select(name, amenity, geometry) %>%
  drop_na(name, amenity)

nrow(amenity_point)
table(amenity_point$amenity)
head(amenity_point)
```

## Visualize OSM Data

`leaflet` is aimed at *interactive* web maps: popups, pan/zoom, a shareable HTML file. `tmap`/`ggplot2` (used throughout earlier labs) are the usual choice for *static*, publication-quality figures. A single `leaflet()` + `addTiles()` + `addCircleMarkers()` chain is a fast way to get a quick interactive look before you invest in custom styling.

```{r}
# Fastest possible interactive preview.
leaflet(data = amenity_point) %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addCircleMarkers()
```

### Get a Free CARTO API Key

CARTO's basemap tiles (used below for their light, low-contrast look) now require a free API key -- unauthenticated requests come back with a visible "API KEY REQUIRED" watermark across the map. This includes leaflet's built-in `providers$CartoDB.Positron`, since it points at the same CARTO tile servers. Getting a key is quick and does **not** require creating a CARTO account:

1. Go to [carto.com/basemaps/apikey](https://carto.com/basemaps/apikey).
2. Fill out the short form: your email, the domain where you'll host the map (your GitHub Pages domain is fine, e.g. `your-username.github.io`), and a one-line project description (e.g. "class assignment").
3. CARTO emails you a key, usually within a few minutes. The free tier covers 5 million tile requests/month -- far more than this lab needs.
4. Paste your key into `CARTO_API_KEY` below.

**Why CARTO and not Mapbox?** Mapbox also issues free API tokens, and token creation there is instant (no email wait at all) -- but Mapbox requires a credit card on file to unlock its free tier, even if you're never charged. CARTO's signup needs no card. For a whole class getting a key, that's worth more than saving a few minutes.

```{r}
# Replace with your own key from carto.com/basemaps/apikey
CARTO_API_KEY <- 'YOUR_KEY_HERE'
```

### Build the Full Map

`leaflet()` builds a map object that you keep adding layers to with the pipe. We chain three layers onto one map, each tagged with a `group=` name so `addLayersControl()` can toggle them independently:

- **buildings** -- solid dark grey polygons, added with `addPolygons()`
- **roads** -- black lines, added with `addPolylines()`
- **amenities** -- circle markers colored by the `amenity` column, added with `addCircleMarkers()`, plus a popup showing the name and type

```{r}
# CartoDB Positron: the {z}/{x}/{y}/{r} placeholders are filled in by Leaflet.js itself
# at render time, not by R, so they stay as plain text here -- only the API key is
# substituted.
tile_url <- paste0('https://{s}.basemaps.cartocdn.com/light_all/{z}/{x}/{y}{r}.png?key=', CARTO_API_KEY)

# required attribution for using the map tiles
map_attr <- '&copy; <a href="https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright">OpenStreetMap</a> contributors &copy; <a href="https://carto.com/attributions">CARTO</a>'

# Assign one color per amenity type for the circle markers and legend.
amenity_colors <- c(
  "restaurant" = "red",
  "fast_food" = "blue",
  "cafe" = "darkgreen"
)

m <- leaflet(data = amenity_point) %>%
  # Basemap: a custom urlTemplate takes the place of addProviderTiles() so the API
  # key can be inserted. Leaving group unset here keeps the basemap out of the
  # layer control below.
  addTiles(urlTemplate = tile_url, attribution = map_attr) %>%
  # Buildings: solid dark grey polygons with no border.
  addPolygons(
    data = building_polygons,
    fillColor = 'darkgrey',
    color = NA,
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    group = 'buildings'
  ) %>%
  # Roads: black lines.
  addPolylines(
    data = roads_lines,
    color = 'black',
    weight = 1.5,
    opacity = 0.7,
    group = 'roads'
  ) %>%
  # Amenities: colored by amenity type, with a popup showing the name and type.
  addCircleMarkers(
    lng = st_coordinates(amenity_point)[,1],
    lat = st_coordinates(amenity_point)[,2],
    popup = ~paste0("<b>", name, "</b><br>", amenity),
    radius = 5,
    color = ~unname(amenity_colors[amenity]),
    fillOpacity = 0.8,
    group = 'amenities'
  ) %>%
  addLegend(
    "bottomright",
    colors = amenity_colors,
    labels = names(amenity_colors),
    title = "Amenity Type",
    opacity = 1
  ) %>%
  # Let users toggle the buildings, roads, and amenities layers independently.
  addLayersControl(
    overlayGroups = c('buildings', 'roads', 'amenities'),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  )

m
```

Zoom, pan, and click markers to open popups. Use the layer control (top right) to toggle buildings, roads, and amenities.

Leaflet can do much more than this! Explore the package's [Articles](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/) for many more powerful examples, such as:

- [Choropleths](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/choropleths.html): color polygons or regions by a data variable (e.g. population density, rates, etc.)
- [Markers](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/markers.html): custom icons and marker clustering
- [Popups and Labels](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/popups.html): standalone popups and hover labels beyond what's shown above
- [Raster Images](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/raster.html): overlay raster/image data on the map
- [Show/Hide Layers](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/showhide.html): programmatically or interactively control which layers are visible
- [Using Leaflet with Shiny](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/articles/shiny.html): build fully interactive apps with dropdown filters, dynamic updates, and more

You'll find many quick examples and patterns in the documentation!

## Export and Host on GitHub Pages

`saveWidget()` writes a standalone HTML file. Use `selfcontained = TRUE` so all JavaScript and CSS are embedded in one file, which works well for GitHub Pages. If you double-click on the file exported in your local folder, you can see and interact with it in your browser. This is a local copy, meaning that you can see it, but you cannot share a link for others to see. To make it sharable, you will have to host it online and we recommend **GitHub Pages** because it provides free hosting service.

```{r}
# html_file <- 'lab9_map.html'
# saveWidget(m, file = html_file, selfcontained = TRUE)
```

### Step 1: Create a GitHub repository

1. Log in to [GitHub](https://github.com) and click **New repository**.
2. Choose a name (e.g. `lab9-osm-map`), set visibility to **Public**, and create the repo.

### Step 2: Add your HTML file and enable GitHub Pages

**Option A -- upload in the browser**

1. In the repo, under the **Quick setup** ssection click the **upload an existing file** link and drag `lab9_map.html` into the upload box that opens.
2. Commit.
3. **Settings** -> **Pages** -> **Deploy from a branch** -> branch **main**, folder **/ (root)** -> Save.
4. After a short wait, open `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/lab9_map.html`.

**Option B -- Git from your computer**

```bash
cd "PATH TO YOUR CURRENT LAB FOLDER"
git clone https://github.com/your-username/lab9-osm-map.git
cd lab9-osm-map
# manually copy lab9_map.html into this folder, then type the following commands
git add lab9_map.html
git commit -m "Add leaflet map"
git push origin main
```

Then enable Pages as in Option A.

### Step 3: Share the link

Use `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/lab9_map.html` in assignments. **Tip:** rename the file to `index.html` in the repo root if you want the map at `https://<your-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/` with no filename.

## Practice Questions

### Q1: Retrieve a new OSM feature

Choose another OSM feature on North Campus -- bicycle parking, bus stops, parking lots, benches, or another amenity -- and retrieve it with `add_osm_feature()`/`add_osm_features()`, following the same two-step process as above (the `bbox` from Step 1 still applies). Use the OSM Wiki or Taginfo to find the right key-value pair.

### Q2: Add it to the map

Add the new feature to the map above as another layer with its own `group=` name (besides amenities, roads, and buildings). Give it a color distinct from the amenities layer, and a tooltip or popup showing at least one useful attribute. Make sure it shows up as a new legend item and its own entry in `addLayersControl()`, and keep all other map aesthetics (e.g. legend style, basemap style, etc.) the same.

### Q3: Export and host

Export your updated map as an HTML file, host it on GitHub Pages, and submit the public URL for the quiz.
